_meta.title: Deep research round 15: research-backed probes for USA, EUR and GLB (25 Oct 2026)
how_to_run: python3 -m p2a sync --no-docs  (and once per scope: --region EUR --universe TOP2500, --region GLB --universe MINVOL1M)
python3 -m p2a try --file research/deep_research_round15.json --route regular --no-sim   # dry run: role fills, validation
python3 -m p2a try --file research/deep_research_round15.json --route regular             # all regions, simulate
python3 -m p2a try --file research/deep_research_round15.json --route regular --region EUR  # one region
_meta.format: Each probe names its region / universe / delay. {name} slots are filled from that scope's live catalog by the probe's own 'roles' specs (ids first, then description patterns) or the roles of research/mechanisms.yaml; a probe whose role finds no field is skipped. Keys the engine does not read (id, theme, fields, risk, papers, evidence, sources) document the research.
_meta.verification: Expressions passed the engine's static analyzer offline (operators, arity, types) with the operator catalog; field ids marked verified come from this repo's earlier probes and notes; roles are unverified until the dry run shows their fills. Paper facts in 'evidence' were checked with web searches on 25 Oct 2026 unless marked 'from memory'. Nothing here has been simulated.
_meta.not_included: MAX/lottery (ts_max does not exist on this account; also a low-volatility tilt); price delay (an illiquidity effect); Stambaugh-Yuan MGMT/PERF factors (a replication thesis found them failing in 88 markets); ideas already measured on this account in rounds 1-14 (FINDINGS.md).

probes.idea: firms issue shares when they are overvalued and buy them back when undervalued; investors under-react to these managerial signals, so net issuers underperform and repurchasers outperform for years (one-year window, Pontiff-Woodgate horizon).
probes.rationale_data: cap and returns (price-volume data, every region): market value growth not explained by returns is net issuance minus payouts
probes.rationale_operators: log(cap / ts_delay(cap, k)) - ts_sum(log(1 + returns), k) is the composite issuance of Daniel-Titman; the minus sign shorts issuers and buys repurchasers
probes.fields: universal price-volume fields
probes.risk: USA issuance is a known factor (model23 net equity issuance reached 0.75 in round 1): watch production correlation
papers: Pontiff and Woodgate (2008) 'Share Issuance and Cross-sectional Returns', Journal of Finance 63(2)
McLean, Pontiff and Watanabe (2009) 'Share issuance and cross-sectional returns: International evidence', Journal of Financial Economics 94(1) 1-17
Daniel and Titman (2006) 'Market Reactions to Tangible and Intangible Information', Journal of Finance 61(4) (composite equity issuance)
Daniel, Hirshleifer and Sun (2020) 'Short- and Long-Horizon Behavioral Factors', Review of Financial Studies 33(4) 1673-1736 (FIN factor)
Manconi, Peyer and Vermaelen (2019) 'Are Buybacks Good for Long-Term Shareholder Value? Evidence from Buybacks around the World', JFQA 54(5) 1899-1935 (2019 Sharpe best paper award)
probes.evidence: 41 non-U.S. countries: issuance predicts returns more significantly than size or momentum, for small and large firms, driven by weak returns after issuance (McLean et al. 2009). Buyback announcements in 31 non-U.S. countries earn positive long-run excess returns (Manconi et al. 2019). FIN is one of two behavioral factors that explain a broad set of anomalies (Daniel et al. 2020).

probes.expression: rank(add(ts_sum(ts_delay(returns, 231), 21), ts_sum(ts_delay(returns, 483), 21), ts_sum(ts_delay(returns, 735), 21), ts_sum(ts_delay(returns, 987), 21), ts_sum(ts_delay(returns, 1239), 21), filter=true))
probes.idea: stocks tend to outperform in the same calendar month in which they outperformed in earlier years (earnings announcement timing, fiscal-year flows and recurring demand): the next month's return in each of the last five years predicts this year's.
probes.rationale_data: returns (price-volume data, every region)
probes.rationale_operators: ts_sum(ts_delay(returns, 231 + 252k), 21) is the return over the coming month k+1 years ago; add(..., filter=true) averages the five years and keeps stocks with shorter histories
probes.fields: universal price-volume fields
probes.risk: price-based: check the reference-factor screen; KLN find seasonalities linked to other anomalies
papers: Heston and Sadka (2008) 'Seasonality in the cross-section of stock returns', Journal of Financial Economics 87(2)
Heston and Sadka (2010) 'Seasonality in the Cross Section of Stock Returns: The International Evidence', JFQA 45(5) 1133-1160
Keloharju, Linnainmaa and Nyberg (2016) 'Return Seasonalities', Journal of Finance 71(4) 1557-1590
probes.evidence: Stocks that beat the market in a calendar month keep beating it in that month for up to 5 years in 14 developed markets (Canada, Japan and 12 European countries); global seasonal strategies beat non-seasonal ones by over 1%/month and are weakly correlated across countries (Heston-Sadka 2010). Same-calendar-month selection earns about 13%/year in the U.S. (Keloharju et al. 2016). A 42-market extension finds the effect mainly in advanced markets.

probes.expression: rank(ts_mean(if_else(open > ts_delay(close, 1), if_else(close < open, 1, 0), 0), 21) / ts_mean(ts_mean(if_else(open > ts_delay(close, 1), if_else(close < open, 1, 0), 0), 21), 252))
probes.idea: a month with many days of overnight gains followed by daytime losses is a tug of war between overnight noise traders and daytime arbitrageurs; the arbitrageurs over-correct a persistent overnight price pressure, so the most intense tug of war predicts higher returns.
probes.rationale_data: open and close (price-volume data, every region): the overnight return is open over the previous close, the daytime return close over open
probes.rationale_operators: if_else marks days with a positive overnight and a negative daytime return; ts_mean over 21 days is the month's frequency, divided by its own 12-month average as in the paper; rank orders stocks
probes.fields: universal price-volume fields
probes.risk: U.S. evidence only; dividends and splits create overnight gaps
papers: Akbas, Boehmer, Jiang and Koch (2022) 'Overnight returns, daytime reversals, and future stock returns', Journal of Financial Economics 145(3) 850-875
Lou, Polk and Skouras (2019) 'A tug of war: Overnight versus intraday expected returns', Journal of Financial Economics 134(1) 192-213
probes.evidence: A month with frequent positive overnight returns followed by daytime reversals (noise traders overnight, arbitrageurs by day) predicts higher future returns: daytime arbitrageurs over-correct (Akbas et al.). Overnight/intraday return components behave persistently differently, strongest in large, high-price stocks (Lou et al.). Evidence is U.S.; EUR/GLB are untested ports with universal price fields.

probes.idea: a week of unusually high trading volume makes a stock more visible to investors (Merton's investor recognition), which raises demand and returns over the following month; the premium exists in 41 countries.
probes.rationale_data: volume (price-volume data, every region)
probes.rationale_operators: ts_mean(volume, 5) over the 50 days before it measures abnormal weekly volume; group_rank by country; decay 6 holds the position for about a month
probes.fields: universal price-volume fields
papers: Kaniel, Ozoguz and Starks (2012) 'The high volume return premium: Cross-country evidence', Journal of Financial Economics 103(2) 255-279
Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin (2001) 'The High-Volume Return Premium', Journal of Finance 56(3)
probes.evidence: Stocks with unusually high trading volume over a week earn higher returns over the next month in 41 developed and emerging countries; not explained by risk or liquidity, larger where visibility changes more (investor recognition). On this account the U.S. version failed (round 8), so it is tried in EUR and GLB only.

probes.idea: momentum in firm-specific (risk-model residual) returns, skipping the last month and scaled by residual volatility: investors under-react to firm news, and the residual version avoids the factor crashes of raw momentum; it works even in Japan.
probes.rationale_data: the risk model's specific (residual) return
probes.rationale_operators: (ts_sum(r, 252) - ts_sum(r, 21)) / ts_std_dev(r, 252) is the 12-1 month residual return over its volatility
probes.fields: role: residual_return (coverage floor 0.7 for this region)
probes.risk: momentum family: check its exposure to the momentum reference factor
papers: Blitz, Huij and Martens (2011) 'Residual momentum', Journal of Empirical Finance 18(3)
Blitz, Hanauer and Vidojevic (2020) 'The idiosyncratic momentum anomaly', International Review of Economics and Finance
probes.evidence: Idiosyncratic momentum earns robust returns across developed and emerging markets, including Japan where ordinary momentum fails; not explained by crash risk; long-run dynamics fit under-reaction.

probes.idea: cash-based operating profitability, which leaves accruals out, predicts returns better than accrual-based profitability and subsumes the accrual anomaly.
probes.rationale_data: operating cash flow and total assets (fundamental data)
probes.rationale_operators: cash flow from operations over total assets, carried between reports with ts_backfill
probes.fields: roles: check the fills with --no-sim first
papers: Novy-Marx (2013) 'The other side of value: The gross profitability premium', Journal of Financial Economics 108(1)
Ball, Gerakos, Linnainmaa and Nikolaev (2016) 'Accruals, cash flows, and operating profitability in the cross section of stock returns', Journal of Financial Economics 121(1)
Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen (2019) 'Quality minus junk', Review of Accounting Studies 24
Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen (2023) 'Is There a Replication Crisis in Finance?', Journal of Finance 78(5)
probes.evidence: Cash-based operating profitability beats accrual-inclusive profitability and subsumes the accrual anomaly (Ball et al.); the profitability premium and the cash-based advantage hold internationally (Huber-Hanauer working paper). Quality is priced across 24 countries (AFP); JKP's 93-country data replicate the quality theme out of sample.

probes.idea: anomaly returns concentrate in the month after the information is released and decay soon after: hold the cash-profitability signal only while the latest report is fresh (up to about 6 weeks old), and drop it once stale.
probes.rationale_data: operating cash flow and total assets (fundamental data); days since the cash-flow value last changed
probes.rationale_operators: trade_when enters while days_from_last_change(...) <= 42, holds, and exits after 63 days
probes.fields: roles: check the fills with --no-sim first
probes.risk: fewer stocks hold positions at any time; compare with the ungated twin
papers: Bowles, Reed, Ringgenberg and Thornock (2024) 'Anomaly Time', Journal of Finance 79(5)
Engelberg, McLean and Pontiff (2018) 'Anomalies and News', Journal of Finance 73(5) 1971-2001
probes.evidence: Anomaly returns concentrate in the first month after the information is released and decay soon after (Bowles et al.); anomaly returns are 50% higher on news days and six times higher on earnings days (Engelberg et al., 97 anomalies). The probe holds a fundamental signal only while it is fresh.

probes.idea: firms with high gross profits relative to assets earn more than unprofitable ones at the same price; gross profit is the cleanest accounting measure of economic profitability.
probes.rationale_data: revenue, cost of goods sold and total assets (fundamental data)
probes.rationale_operators: (revenue - COGS) / assets with ts_backfill carrying each annual or quarterly value between reports
probes.fields: roles: check the fills with --no-sim first
papers: Novy-Marx (2013) 'The other side of value: The gross profitability premium', Journal of Financial Economics 108(1)
Ball, Gerakos, Linnainmaa and Nikolaev (2016) 'Accruals, cash flows, and operating profitability in the cross section of stock returns', Journal of Financial Economics 121(1)

La Porta (1996) 'Expectations and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 51(5)
probes.evidence: Stocks with the most optimistic analyst long-term growth forecasts earn lower returns than those with the most pessimistic: analysts over-extrapolate (diagnostic expectations). U.S. evidence; EUR/GLB are ports where the field exists.

probes.idea: analysts' target-price-implied returns are informative relative to industry peers: ranking target price over price within an industry removes analysts' industry-wide optimism and keeps their relative valuation.
probes.rationale_data: consensus analyst target price and the close price

probes.fields: verified id in USA (mean_estimate_targetprice_annual12_tribes); role elsewhere
probes.risk: target over price rises when the price falls: watch the 5-day reversal exposure

Dechow and You (2020) 'Understanding the Determinants of Analyst Target Price Implied Returns', The Accounting Review 95(6)
probes.evidence: Target-price-implied returns are informative relative to industry peers: ranking within an industry removes the industry-wide optimism of analysts (Da-Schaumburg; details from memory, not re-verified this session). Consensus targets implied 22.7% a year against 9.3% realized (Dechow-You draft), so level comparisons across industries are biased.

probes.idea: investors fail to separate bold revisions (away from consensus, new information) from herding ones; the drift after bold upward minus bold downward revisions is the under-priced part of analysts' news.
probes.rationale_data: counts of positive and negative bold FY1 earnings estimates
probes.rationale_operators: ts_backfill carries the counts over a quarter; rank of their difference
probes.fields: verified USA ids (model26 test fixture); role elsewhere

Clement and Tse (2005) 'Financial Analyst Characteristics and Herding Behavior in Forecasting', Journal of Finance 60(1)
probes.evidence: Prices fail to separate high-innovation revisions (moving away from consensus) from herding ones; the drift after informative revisions is larger and is corrected around later announcements (Gleason-Lee). Bold forecasts carry more information than herding ones (Clement-Tse).

probes.idea: uncertainty about risk is disliked: stocks whose implied volatility itself is volatile (high vol-of-vol) underperform those with stable implied volatility, by about 8% a year in the U.S. and Europe.

papers: Baltussen, van Bekkum and van der Grient (2018) 'Unknown Unknowns: Uncertainty About Risk and Stock Returns', JFQA 53(4) 1615-1651
probes.evidence: Stocks with high volatility of implied volatility underperform low ones by about 8%/year in the U.S. and Europe, distinct from at least 20 known predictors. On this account option-surface changes were the most unique information found (IV innovations: one production alpha above 0.5).
